steps.title: An EKS Auto Mode cluster
steps.what: It tells eksctl to create a Kubernetes 1.37 cluster named hello-eks, with Auto Mode turned on.
steps.why: Auto Mode launches, patches, and removes the machines for you. It is not a Kubernetes object, so you never apply it.

steps.title: Load balancer settings
steps.what: It holds settings for the load balancers EKS builds. internet-facing gives them a public address.
steps.why: Without it, the load balancer would be internal, and your browser could not reach it.

steps.title: Who builds the load balancer
steps.what: It tells EKS Auto Mode to build Application Load Balancers for Ingresses that name public-alb.
steps.why: It links each Ingress to the settings in IngressClassParams.

steps.title: A public address for the app
steps.what: It sends every request to the hello Service on port 80. The load balancer checks /healthz, which needs no login.
steps.why: Lab 1 used kubectl port-forward. The Ingress gives the app a real web address instead.

steps.title: What kind of disk to make
steps.what: It tells EKS Auto Mode to make encrypted gp3 EBS volumes.
steps.why: WaitForFirstConsumer waits for a Pod before making the disk. The disk then lands in the same zone as the Pod.

steps.title: Ask for a disk
steps.what: It asks for a 1 GiB disk from the auto-ebs StorageClass. ReadWriteOnce lets one machine use it at a time.
steps.why: The disk outlives any Pod. In lab step 6, the note survives when its Pod is deleted.

steps.title: A name for Pod Identity
steps.what: It creates the notes ServiceAccount in the hello Namespace.
steps.why: Lab step 3 links this name to the hello-notes IAM role. Pods that use it get that role's temporary keys.

steps.title: A script that asks AWS who the Pod is
steps.what: It holds a short script. The script reads the Pod's temporary AWS keys and calls STS GetCallerIdentity.
steps.why: Lab step 7 runs it to prove the Pod acts as the hello-notes role, with no keys stored in Kubernetes.

steps.title: One Pod with the disk and the role
steps.what: It runs one Pod with the disk at /data and the script at /scripts, as the notes ServiceAccount.
steps.why: Recreate stops the old Pod first, because an EBS disk attaches to one machine at a time.

notes.metadata.namespace: The Namespace this object lives in: hello, from Lab 1.
notes.ClusterConfig:apiVersion: The eksctl file format. eksctl reads this file, and Kubernetes never sees it.
notes.ClusterConfig:kind: ClusterConfig describes a whole cluster for eksctl to create.
notes.ClusterConfig:metadata: The cluster's name, Region, version, and tags.
notes.ClusterConfig:metadata.name: The cluster's name in EKS. The clean-up step deletes the cluster by this name.
notes.ClusterConfig:metadata.region: The AWS Region to build the cluster in. The sed command in lab step 1 sets yours.
notes.ClusterConfig:metadata.version: The Kubernetes version. The quotes keep it text, so a version like 1.30 is not read as 1.3.
notes.ClusterConfig:metadata.tags: Tags eksctl adds to the AWS resources it creates.
notes.ClusterConfig:metadata.tags.lab: A tag that marks the AWS resources eksctl creates for this lab.
notes.ClusterConfig:autoModeConfig.enabled: Turns on Auto Mode. EKS then manages the machines, load balancers, and block storage for you.
notes.Ingress:metadata.annotations: Extra settings the load balancer reads.
notes.Ingress:metadata.annotations.alb.ingress: The path the load balancer checks on each Pod. /healthz answers without a login.
notes.ConfigMap:data.aws-whoami.sh: A short script. It reads the Pod's temporary AWS keys and asks AWS STS who the Pod is.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.spec.serviceAcc: The ServiceAccount the Pod runs as. Pod Identity gives it the hello-notes role's temporary keys.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.spec.securityCo: Security settings for every container in the Pod.
Kubernetes refuses to start a container that would run as root. This image runs as user 101.
Gives the disk's files to group 101, so the image's normal user can write to it.
notes.IngressClassParams:apiVersion: The API group and version: eks.amazonaws.com/v1, Auto Mode's own.
notes.IngressClass:apiVersion: The API group and version: networking.k8s.io/v1.
notes.Ingress:apiVersion: The API group and version: networking.k8s.io/v1.
notes.Ingress:metadata.name: The Ingress name. kubectl get ingress hello -n hello shows its address.
notes.Ingress:spec.rules[].http.paths[].backen: Port 80, where the hello Service listens.
notes.StorageClass:apiVersion: The API group and version: storage.k8s.io/v1.
notes.PersistentVolumeClaim:apiVersion: The core v1 API, where PersistentVolumeClaims live.
notes.ServiceAccount:metadata.name: The ServiceAccount's name: notes. The Pod Identity link in lab step 3 uses this name.
notes.Deployment:spec.replicas: How many Pods to keep running: one, because the disk attaches to one machine at a time.
notes.Deployment:spec.selector.matchLabels.app: Match Pods whose app label is notes.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.metadata.labels: Every Pod gets the label app: notes, so the selector finds it.
notes.Deployment:spec.template.spec.containers: The same web server image as Lab 1. It includes curl, which the script uses.
CPU the container needs. 1000m equals one CPU, so 50m is a twentieth.
The volume to mount. It matches a name under volumes.
The folder inside the container where the volume appears.

questions.question: What does autoModeConfig.enabled: true change?
answers: EKS starts and manages the machines for you
The cluster gets a public address
questions.explain: Auto Mode starts machines when Pods need them. That is why a new cluster has no nodes yet.

questions.question: Which line does the sed command in lab step 1 change?
questions.explain: sed puts the Region you chose into the file, so eksctl builds the cluster there.

questions.question: Why is the version written as "1.37", in quotes?
answers: eksctl needs every value in quotes
Quotes keep it text, so 1.30 would not become 1.3
Quotes make it the newest version
questions.explain: Without quotes, YAML reads 1.30 as the number 1.3. The quotes keep every version exactly as written.

questions.question: What makes the load balancer reachable from the internet?
questions.explain: internet-facing gives the load balancer a public address. Without it, the load balancer is internal.

questions.question: Why does the notes Deployment use Recreate?
answers: An EBS disk attaches to one machine at a time
questions.explain: Recreate stops the old Pod before starting the new one, so the disk is free to move.

questions.question: Which line lets the notes Pod act as an IAM role?
questions.explain: Pod Identity links the notes ServiceAccount to the hello-notes role. Pods that use it get that role's keys.
